summary: This informational document defines a deterministic procedure for generating digital signatures. The signatures are compatible with standard DSA and ECDSA and verifiers need not know about the procedure. They retain the security properties of normal signatures but can be easier to implement in some environments.

eli5.summary: Normally signing needs a random number each time. This way the number is worked out from the message and key instead, but signatures look normal.

subtitle: How to sign with DSA or ECDSA without a random number generator, by deriving the per-signature value from the key and message.

tldr.problem: DSA and ECDSA need a fresh, high-quality random value k for every signature, which is hard to provide on devices like smartcards and hard to test.
tldr.mechanism: Derive k from the private key and the hashed message using an HMAC-based generator (HMAC_DRBG style), then run the normal DSA or ECDSA signing steps.
tldr.outcome: The signatures are fully compatible with plain DSA and ECDSA, so verifiers need no changes, and signing needs no randomness. Key generation still needs good randomness.

today: RFC 6979 is an Informational, independent-stream RFC, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC Editor states that it makes no statement about the document's value for implementation or deployment.

sections.title: Why Signing Needs Randomness
sections.content:
DSA and ECDSA provide data integrity and verifiable authenticity. Each time they sign, they need a fresh random value called k, chosen uniformly from a set of modular integers by a cryptographically secure process. Even slight biases in that process may be turned into attacks on the signature scheme.

That requirement hinders deployment in some architectures, especially embedded systems such as smartcards. There, RSA used as in PKCS #1 with type 1 padding is often preferred even though it costs more computation, because it is deterministic. Randomized signing is also harder to test: automatic tests cannot reliably detect whether the source of randomness is good enough, so failures can show up only after deployment and a successful attack.

The fix is to generate k deterministically. The mapping from messages to k values must still be computationally indistinguishable from a randomly chosen function for anyone who does not know the private key.
sections.eli5: Some tiny devices cannot roll good dice, and nobody can easily check if the dice are fair. A bad roll can leak the secret, so it is safer to avoid dice altogether.

sections.title: Standard DSA and ECDSA Signing
sections.content:
The RFC first restates how signing works. The private key is an integer x in the range [1, q-1]. The message is hashed with a function H, and the result is turned into an integer h = bits2int(H(m)) mod q.

Then a value k in [1, q-1] is chosen. A value r is computed from k (for DSA, r = g^k mod p mod q; for ECDSA, the X coordinate of the point kG reduced modulo q). If r is zero, a new k is needed. Finally s = (h+x*r)/k mod q, and the pair (r, s) is the signature.

Three helper conversions are defined, all driven by qlen, the bit length of q. bits2int truncates or left-pads a bit string to qlen bits and reads it as a big-endian integer. int2octets encodes an integer below q as rlen bits, where rlen is qlen rounded up to a multiple of 8. bits2octets applies bits2int, reduces the result modulo q, then applies int2octets.
sections.eli5: Signing mixes your secret, the message fingerprint and a one-time number. The helper steps just squeeze all these numbers into the right size.

sections.title: Generating k Deterministically
sections.content:
Deterministic (EC)DSA is the standard signing process, except that k comes from the procedure below. It uses HMAC with the same hash function H that hashes the message.

  • Hash the message: h1 = H(m).
  • Set V to a string of 0x01 octets and K to a string of 0x00 octets, each as long as the hash output (32 octets for SHA-256).
  • Update K and V twice, first with K = HMAC_K(V || 0x00 || int2octets(x) || bits2octets(h1)), then with the same input but the internal octet 0x01, each followed by V = HMAC_K(V).
  • Loop: build T by repeatedly applying V = HMAC_K(V) and appending V until T has at least qlen bits, then set k = bits2int(T).
  • If k is in [1, q-1] and gives a nonzero r, it is accepted. Otherwise, compute K = HMAC_K(V || 0x00) and V = HMAC_K(V) and try again.

The candidate is compared to q, never reduced modulo q, because reduction would introduce biases that harm security.

The RFC also gives an equivalent description using the HMAC_DRBG generator from NIST SP 800-90A: the private key encoding acts as the entropy string, bits2octets(H(m)) acts as the nonce, and the reseed function is never called. A zero r is so improbable that the RFC says the retry path will not be triggered in practice.
sections.eli5: Take your secret and the message, stir them through a mixing machine over and over, and use what comes out as the one-time number. The same message and secret always give the same number.

sections.title: Rationale and Variants
sections.content:
The process follows the approved k generation in Annex D of ANSI X9.62 with HMAC_DRBG, but seeds it with the private key x and the hashed message. The RFC argues this meets the entropy requirement because x is generated with at least as much entropy as the security level needs. It uses bits2octets(H(m)) so the scheme works in systems that send only an already truncated hash to the signature engine.

Several variants are listed, but they are not "deterministic (EC)DSA" and can no longer be checked against the published test vectors:

  • Using H(m) directly instead of bits2octets(H(m)); the RFC says this introduces no vulnerability.
  • Appending additional non-repeating data k' (such as a signature counter or monotonic clock) for protocols that want non-deterministic signatures without a strong random source.
  • Using separate secret data, or a value derived from a master secret, instead of x as HMAC input; this may ease formal proofs but costs storage or breaks compatibility with existing keys.
  • Using two different hash functions for the message and for HMAC; security is then limited by the weaker one.
sections.eli5: You can tweak the recipe, for example by adding a counter, but then your results will no longer match the official answer sheet.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Key generation still absolutely requires a strong random source. Where deterministic signing is used because randomness is unavailable, the private key must be generated elsewhere (the RFC suggests a smartcard keyed in a factory under controlled conditions) and imported. Key storage and disposal are not addressed.

Removing the random source and allowing test-vector checks both help avoid hard-to-test failures. Determinism can also help detect duplicates, since the same data signed with the same key gives the same signature. On the other hand, lack of randomization may hurt advanced protocols, for example some anonymity-related voting schemes. As a rule of thumb, deterministic DSA or ECDSA is fine wherever the protocol would tolerate deterministic RSA with PKCS #1 type 1 padding. The RFC names TLS, SSH, CMS and X.509 public key infrastructures among the suitable protocols.

The scheme's security rests on HMAC behaving as a pseudorandom function. One open point is the "double use" of x, as the signing key and as HMAC input, which the RFC judges reasonable given the lack of common structure between HMAC and discrete logarithms. Determinism may help an attacker in some side-channel attacks, so implementations SHOULD use defensive measures against leaking the private key.
sections.eli5: You still need good dice once, when you first make your secret key. After that the recipe is safe, but you should still hide your device from snoops watching its power use or timing.

items.title: Signatures
items.text: Fully compatible with plain DSA and ECDSA; verifiers need not be aware.

items.title: Key pairs
items.text: Key pair generation is not altered; existing private keys work.

items.title: Storage
items.text: No extra secret or public value to store.

items.title: Inputs
items.text: Applied over the same hash of the message as plain DSA and ECDSA.
